result: EPIC is a computational method that estimates the fraction of cancer and immune cell types from bulk tumor RNA-Seq data by modeling gene expression as a linear combination of reference profiles from non-malignant cell types, incorporating cell-type-specific mRNA content normalization, and allowing for uncharacterized cell types (primarily cancer cells) through the use of signature genes with negligible expression in cancer cells.
evaluation: Claims C2-C5, C20-C21, C26, C37-C44, C81-C82, and C113-C120 collectively describe the EPIC algorithm's design and mathematical framework. The method is well-documented with clear mathematical formulations (equations provided in Materials and methods), experimental validation of mRNA content measurements (C44, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and signature gene selection criteria (C43, Appendix 1—table 1). The algorithmic approach is internally consistent and builds on established computational principles (C116).

result: Reference gene expression profiles for circulating immune cells (CD4 T, CD8 T, B, NK, monocytes, neutrophils) were constructed from RNA-Seq data of sorted cells from multiple studies, with principal component analysis confirming that samples cluster by cell type rather than experimental batch, and profiles were built using median TPM counts and interquartile ranges per gene and cell type.
evaluation: Claims C27-C31 and C133-C138 describe the construction of circulating immune cell reference profiles with appropriate quality control (PCA analysis in Figure 1C showing cell-type clustering, C28-C29, C134). The use of data from multiple independent studies (C27) and the statistical approach (median and IQR, C30-C31, C135-C136) are appropriate for building robust reference profiles. The data sources are properly cited and the methodology is clearly described.

result: Reference gene expression profiles for tumor-infiltrating cells (CD4 T, CD8 T, B, NK, macrophages, CAFs, endothelial cells) were established from single-cell RNA-Seq data of melanoma patients, with PCA showing cell-type clustering, and profiles built using mean and standard deviation to account for single-cell RNA-Seq characteristics.
evaluation: Claims C32-C36 and C141 describe the construction of tumor-infiltrating cell reference profiles from single-cell RNA-Seq data (Tirosh et al., 2016). The PCA analysis (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) confirms cell-type clustering (C36). The methodological adaptation to use mean/standard deviation instead of median/IQR (C141) is justified by the nature of single-cell RNA-Seq data with dropout events. The approach is well-documented and appropriately adapted to the data type.

result: EPIC was validated in blood samples using three datasets with flow cytometry measurements, showing very accurate predictions (high correlation, low RMSE) that outperformed other methods, with mRNA content renormalization being important for accuracy, and the method remaining robust when T cell reference profiles were removed.
evaluation: Claims C45-C55 describe comprehensive validation in blood samples with quantitative metrics (Figure 2A-C, Figure 2—figure supplements 1-4). The validation includes appropriate comparisons with multiple existing methods (C47), demonstrates the importance of mRNA renormalization (C48-C49, Figure 2C), and tests robustness to missing reference profiles (C55, Figure 2—figure supplement 4). The statistical analyses are appropriate with correlation coefficients, RMSE values, and significance testing. The validation is rigorous and well-controlled.

result: EPIC was validated in melanoma lymph node samples from four stage III patients using parallel flow cytometry and RNA-Seq analysis, showing remarkable agreement between predicted and observed cell fractions for all cell types including cancer cells, with predictions falling nearly on the y=x line and low RMSE.
evaluation: Claims C6, C22, C56-C60, and C121-C126 describe a rigorous experimental validation with appropriate ethical approval (C121-C122), clear sample processing protocols (C123-C125), and parallel measurements on the same samples (C57). The results show strong quantitative agreement (Figure 3A, C58-C59) with the critical demonstration that cancer cell proportions can be accurately predicted without prior reference profiles (C60). The data are publicly available (C126, GSE93722), supporting reproducibility. This represents a key validation of EPIC's core capability.

result: EPIC predictions showed significant correlation with immunohistochemistry data from colon cancer primary tumors for most immune cell types except CD8 T cells, though the validation is limited by the inability to use identical samples for both gene expression and IHC analyses.
evaluation: Claims C7, C23, C61, and C107 describe validation using publicly available IHC data (Becht et al., 2016, Figure 3B). While significant correlations were observed for most cell types, CD8 T cells showed no significant correlation (C61). The authors acknowledge that different samples had to be used for gene expression and IHC due to technical incompatibility (C107), which introduces uncertainty. The validation is less definitive than the flow cytometry validation due to this limitation and the restricted number of cell types assayed.

result: EPIC predictions were consistent with observed cell fractions from single-cell RNA-Seq data of melanoma samples, with predictions for all cell types including cancer cells falling nearly on the y=x line, using a leave-one-out procedure to avoid circularity.
evaluation: Claims C8, C24, C62-C64 describe validation using single-cell RNA-Seq data (Tirosh et al., 2016, Figure 3C) with appropriate methodological controls. The leave-one-out procedure (C64) prevents circular analysis by ensuring reference profiles and test samples come from different patients. The results show strong quantitative agreement for both relative and absolute proportions (C63), including cancer cells without reference profiles. This independent validation using a different technology strengthens confidence in EPIC's accuracy.

result: Predictions using tumor-infiltrating cell reference profiles showed similar overall accuracy to circulating cell profiles, but improved predictions for CD8 T cells and macrophages in primary tumors and non-lymph node metastases (not lymph node metastases), with the monocyte profile serving as an effective proxy for macrophages, and tumor-infiltrating profiles enabling prediction of CAFs and endothelial cells.
evaluation: Claims C65-C69, C86-C89, C139-C140 describe systematic comparisons between circulating and tumor-infiltrating cell reference profiles across multiple validation datasets (Figures 3-4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The tissue-specific differences in prediction accuracy (C67, C86) are biologically plausible given the activation states of immune cells in different contexts (C87). The use of monocyte profiles as a proxy for macrophages is justified and validated (C139-C140). The recommendations for profile selection based on tumor type (C88-C89) are data-driven and practical.

result: EPIC showed improved accuracy compared to ISOpure and other cell fraction prediction methods across all validation datasets, particularly when considering all cell types together, though some methods (MCPcounter, TIMER) showed similar accuracy for relative proportions of specific cell types, and ESTIMATE scores showed lower correlations and less quantitative interpretability than EPIC.
evaluation: Claims C70-C77 describe comprehensive benchmarking against multiple existing methods (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplements 1-5). The comparisons are fair and acknowledge both strengths and limitations of different methods (C72-C74). The statistical analyses are appropriate with correlation coefficients and RMSE values. The assessment of ESTIMATE's limitations (C75-C77) is supported by the data. The benchmarking demonstrates EPIC's advantages while providing balanced evaluation of alternative approaches.

result: Exploratory analysis of T cell subsets (Treg and Thelper) showed significant but lower correlations than for major cell types, with neither EPIC nor CIBERSORT performing well for Treg prediction, likely due to high transcriptional similarity between Thelper and Treg and low Treg abundance (<10%).
evaluation: Claims C78-C80, C94-C95 describe exploratory analysis of T cell subset prediction (Figure 5—figure supplement 6). The lower accuracy is appropriately attributed to biological factors: high transcriptional similarity between cell types (C94) and low abundance (C95, Supplementary file 3E). The comparison with CIBERSORT (C80) shows this is a general limitation of deconvolution methods for similar cell types. The authors appropriately characterize this as reaching the limits of cell fraction prediction methods and do not overstate the results.

result: Cell fraction predictions have known limitations for cell types present at very low frequency (detection limit ~8% absolute error based on RMSE) and for cell types with high transcriptional similarity, with gene set enrichment approaches potentially more appropriate for such cases.
evaluation: Claims C90-C93, C96 discuss limitations of cell fraction prediction methods with appropriate supporting evidence. The 8% error estimate (C91) is derived from validation data (Figure 3, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and is consistent with other studies (C92). The discussion of limitations for low-frequency cells (C90) and transcriptionally similar cells (C93) is supported by the NK cell and Treg prediction results. The recommendation for alternative approaches (C96) is reasonable and appropriately cautious.

result: EPIC can be broadly applied to most solid tumors as validated in melanoma and colorectal samples, but is not suitable for hematological malignancies, with predictions for uncharacterized cells potentially including non-malignant epithelial cells in addition to cancer cells, and the method offering advantages over exome-based approaches by not requiring both exome and RNA-Seq data.
evaluation: Claims C83-C84, C97-C99 discuss the applicability and limitations of EPIC. The broad applicability to solid tumors (C83) is supported by validation in two tumor types (melanoma and colorectal). The exclusion of hematological malignancies (C84) is logically justified by the algorithmic assumption that cancer cells don't express immune markers (C82). The potential inclusion of epithelial cells in the uncharacterized fraction (C97) is an honest acknowledgment of a limitation. The comparison with exome-based methods (C98-C99) is reasonable and highlights practical advantages.

result: While single-cell RNA-Seq provides richer data than bulk deconvolution, it faces technical challenges including cell death, transcript dropout, and potential processing biases, making bulk tumor gene expression analysis likely to remain widely used, with EPIC demonstrating how single-cell data from a few patients can improve predictions for other patients through detailed validation with flow cytometry, IHC, and single-cell RNA-Seq.
evaluation: Claims C100-C106, C108 provide context for EPIC's role relative to single-cell RNA-Seq technology. The discussion of single-cell RNA-Seq advantages (C100-C101) and limitations (C102-C103) is balanced and supported by appropriate citations. The prediction about continued use of bulk RNA-Seq (C104) is reasonable speculation based on current technical limitations. The summary of EPIC's validation (C106, C108) accurately reflects the comprehensive experimental work presented. This contextualizes EPIC's contribution appropriately.

result: EPIC is freely available as an R package (version 1.1) on GitHub for academic non-commercial use and as a web application at http://epic.gfellerlab.org, with pre-compiled reference profiles from circulating or tumor-infiltrating cells or user-provided profiles.
evaluation: Claims C109-C112 describe the availability and accessibility of EPIC. The specific version number (C112), GitHub repository, and web application URL (C110) are provided. The licensing terms (C111) and usage options (C109) are clearly stated. This information supports reproducibility and broad adoption of the method. The claims are straightforward statements of fact about software availability.

result: mRNA content per cell type was measured for immune cells from sorted peripheral blood, and cancer cell mRNA content was estimated using forward scatter width from flow cytometry as a proxy for cell size, with cancer cells showing similar mRNA content to B, NK, and T cells, leading to use of 0.4 pg mRNA per cancer cell in EPIC.
evaluation: Claims C127-C131 describe the experimental measurement of mRNA content (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The approach for immune cells is direct measurement (C127-C129), while cancer cell estimation uses forward scatter width as a validated proxy for cell size and mRNA content (C130, with appropriate citations to Padovan-Merhar et al., 2015; Tzur et al., 2011). The resulting parameter value (C131) is based on experimental observations. The methodology is appropriate and well-justified, though the cancer cell estimate is indirect.

result: RNA-seq reads were aligned to the human genome (hg19) and TPM quantification was performed using RSEM version 1.2.19, Bowtie2 version 2.2.4, and Samtools version 1.2.
evaluation: Claim C132 provides specific details about the bioinformatics pipeline with version numbers for all software tools and appropriate citations. This level of detail supports computational reproducibility. The tools used (RSEM, Bowtie2, Samtools) are standard and appropriate for RNA-Seq analysis. This is a straightforward methodological claim that is well-documented.

result: The manuscript provides background context that immune cells infiltrating tumors impact tumor progression and therapy response, gene expression analysis is widely used with extensive public data available, but flow cytometry/IHC measurements are rarely performed alongside gene expression, and existing bioinformatics methods have limitations including lack of quantitative information about both cancer and non-malignant cell types, reliance on microarray-based circulating immune cell profiles, and lack of experimental validation in solid tumors.
evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C19 provide background and motivation for the study. These claims are supported by appropriate citations to established literature (C1, C9-C10, C12, C14-C15, C17-C18) or represent reasonable assessments of the field (C13, C16, C19). The characterization of existing methods' limitations (C14-C19) is fair and supported by citations. This background appropriately motivates the development of EPIC and is consistent with the state of the field.

result: All three validation datasets (flow cytometry, IHC, single-cell RNA-Seq) showed that very accurate predictions of both cancer and non-malignant cell type proportions could be obtained even in the absence of a priori information about cancer cells.
evaluation: Claim C25 is a summary statement that integrates results from multiple validation approaches (C6-C8, C22-C24, C58, C61-C62). The claim is supported by the quantitative results shown in Figures 3-4, with high correlations and low RMSE values across all three validation datasets. The key point about predicting cancer cell proportions without reference profiles (C60, C62) is particularly well-demonstrated. This summary accurately reflects the validation results.

result: Previous computational work showed that proportions of uncharacterized cells can be inferred using genes not expressed by those cells, and cell-specific signature genes are well established and widely used in flow cytometry for cell sorting.
evaluation: Claims C116-C117 provide theoretical and practical justification for EPIC's approach. C116 cites previous computational work (Clarke et al., 2010; Gosink et al., 2007) supporting the mathematical feasibility of the approach. C117 notes that signature genes are established in flow cytometry practice, providing biological validation for the concept. These claims appropriately ground EPIC's methodology in prior work and established practice.
